notes:
1. Poverty — Meaning

  • Poverty is a condition in which individuals or households lack adequate resources and capabilities to achieve an acceptable standard of living.
  • Poverty is broader than shortage of income alone.
  • Deprivation can simultaneously affect food, housing, education, health, water, sanitation, electricity, employment, finance and social security.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poverty → Monetary Deprivation + Capability Deprivation

2. Monetary vs Multidimensional Poverty

Monetary poverty:

  • Measures whether income or consumption falls below a specified threshold.

Multidimensional poverty:

  • Measures simultaneous deprivation across several dimensions of well-being.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Income Poverty ≠ Complete Human Deprivation

3. Absolute Poverty

  • Absolute poverty refers to inability to meet a specified minimum standard of basic needs.

Basic requirements may include:

  • Food.
  • Clothing.
  • Housing.
  • Essential services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Absolute Poverty → Minimum Basic-Needs Threshold

4. Relative Poverty

  • Relative poverty compares an individual's economic position with the prevailing living standards of society.
  • It is closely connected with inequality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Relative Poverty → Position Compared with Society

5. Absolute vs Relative Poverty

  • Absolute poverty asks → Can minimum basic needs be met?
  • Relative poverty asks → How far below prevailing social standards is the person?
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Absolute Poverty ≠ Relative Poverty

6. Poverty Line

  • A poverty line is a specified threshold used to classify persons as poor or non-poor under a particular methodology.
  • It is not a permanent rupee amount because prices and purchasing power change over time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poverty Line → Measurement Threshold

7. Consumption-Based Poverty Measurement

  • India historically relied substantially on household consumption expenditure rather than reported income for monetary-poverty estimation.
  • Consumption can be more stable than income for agricultural and self-employed households.

8. MPCE

  • MPCE stands for Monthly Per Capita Expenditure.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPCE = Monthly Household Consumption Expenditure ÷ Household Size

9. MPCE vs Poverty Line

  • MPCE measures consumption expenditure per person.
  • A poverty line is the threshold against which consumption may be compared.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MPCE ≠ Poverty Line

10. BPL — Below Poverty Line

  • BPL means Below Poverty Line.
  • Administrative BPL beneficiary identification should not automatically be equated with statistical poverty estimation.
  • Government schemes may use separate eligibility criteria.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

BPL Beneficiary Status ≠ Statistical Poverty Status

11. International Poverty Line

According to the supplied source:

  • The World Bank updated its international extreme-poverty line in June 2025 to US$3.00 per person per day in 2021 PPP terms.
📌 Must-Memorise

International Extreme-Poverty Line in Source → US$3.00, 2021 PPP

12. PPP — Purchasing Power Parity

  • PPP stands for Purchasing Power Parity.
  • PPP-based international poverty thresholds should not be converted using ordinary market exchange rates.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

PPP Conversion ≠ Normal Foreign-Exchange Conversion

13. Dadabhai Naoroji — Early Poverty Analysis

  • Dadabhai Naoroji was among the earliest Indian thinkers to systematically analyse poverty under colonial rule.
  • He connected poverty with colonial exploitation and the drain of wealth.
  • His famous work Poverty and Un-British Rule in India was published in 1901.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dadabhai Naoroji → Poverty and Un-British Rule in India → 1901

14. Evolution of Poverty Measurement

India's poverty-measurement evolution can broadly be remembered as:

Basic Needs

→ Calorie Norms

→ Consumption Basket

→ Broader Non-Food Needs

→ Multidimensional Poverty

15. Y. K. Alagh Task Force

  • The Y. K. Alagh Task Force developed an influential calorie-linked poverty-measurement approach in the late 1970s.
  • It linked poverty lines to consumption expenditure required to meet specified calorie norms.

16. Alagh — Calorie Norms

Commonly cited norms were approximately:

  • Rural → 2,400 calories per person per day.
  • Urban → 2,100 calories per person per day.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alagh → 2400 Rural | 2100 Urban

17. Why Rural Calorie Norm Was Higher

  • The higher rural norm reflected assumptions of greater physical activity in rural occupations.

18. Lakdawala Expert Group

  • The Expert Group chaired by D. T. Lakdawala submitted its report in 1993.
  • It retained the calorie-linked approach while introducing State-specific poverty lines.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lakdawala → 1993

19. Lakdawala — Key Contribution

  • State-specific poverty lines recognised differences in price levels across States.
  • Separate rural and urban price indices were used broadly for updating poverty lines.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lakdawala → State-Specific Poverty Lines

20. Limitation of Calorie-Based Poverty Measurement

Purely calorie-linked measurement became less satisfactory because households also incur essential expenditure on:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Transport.
  • Housing.
  • Other non-food requirements.

21. Tendulkar Committee

  • The Expert Group headed by Suresh D. Tendulkar submitted its report in 2009.
  • It marked an important methodological shift in Indian poverty measurement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tendulkar Committee → 2009

22. Tendulkar — Major Methodological Shift

  • Tendulkar moved away from mechanically linking poverty lines to fixed calorie norms.
  • It recognised essential non-food spending, particularly health and education.
  • It used an all-India urban poverty-line basket as an important reference for comparable poverty lines.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tendulkar → Shift Away from Fixed Calorie Anchoring

23. Tendulkar Poverty Lines — 2011–12

At 2011–12 prices:

  • Rural → approximately ₹816 per person per month.
  • Urban → approximately ₹1,000 per person per month.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

₹816 and ₹1,000 → 2011–12 Prices, Not Current Poverty Lines

24. Tendulkar Poverty Ratio — 2011–12

Official estimates under the Tendulkar methodology:

  • Rural → 25.7%.
  • Urban → 13.7%.
  • India overall → 21.9%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tendulkar 2011–12 → India Poverty Ratio 21.9%

25. Poverty Decline — Tendulkar Series

  • The national poverty ratio declined from 37.2% in 2004–05 to 21.9% in 2011–12 under the broad Tendulkar methodology.

26. Rangarajan Committee

  • The Planning Commission constituted a new Expert Group headed by C. Rangarajan in 2012.
  • It submitted its report in 2014.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rangarajan Committee → Report 2014

27. Rangarajan — Poverty Basket

The Rangarajan methodology included normative requirements relating to:

  • Food.
  • Clothing.
  • House rent.
  • Conveyance.
  • Education.
  • It also included other non-food expenditure.

28. Rangarajan — Nutritional Approach

  • Rangarajan considered calories along with protein and fat requirements.
  • It used separate rural and urban poverty baskets.

29. Rangarajan Poverty Lines — 2011–12

Proposed thresholds:

  • Rural → ₹972 per person per month.
  • Urban → ₹1,407 per person per month.

For a family of five:

  • Rural → approximately ₹4,860 per month.
  • Urban → approximately ₹7,035 per month.

30. Rangarajan Poverty Ratio — 2011–12

The Rangarajan methodology estimated:

  • Rural → 30.9%.
  • Urban → 26.4%.
  • India overall → 29.5%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rangarajan 2011–12 → 29.5%

31. Tendulkar vs Rangarajan

Tendulkar:

  • Report → 2009.
  • Rural line → ₹816.
  • Urban line → ₹1,000.
  • India poverty ratio → 21.9%.

Rangarajan:

  • Report → 2014.
  • Rural line → ₹972.
  • Urban line → ₹1,407.
  • India poverty ratio → 29.5%.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tendulkar and Rangarajan Estimates Are Not Interchangeable

32. Why Rangarajan Estimated More Poor Persons

  • Rangarajan proposed higher poverty thresholds.
  • Other things equal, a higher poverty line classifies a larger number of persons as poor.

33. Poverty Headcount Ratio

  • The Poverty Headcount Ratio measures the proportion of the population classified as poor.
📌 Must-Memorise

Headcount Ratio = Poor Population ÷ Total Population × 100

34. Limitation of Headcount Ratio

  • Headcount ratio tells how many people are poor.
  • It does not show how far below the poverty line they are.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Headcount Ratio → Incidence, Not Depth

35. Poverty Gap

  • Poverty gap measures the average shortfall of poor people's income or consumption from the poverty line.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poverty Gap → Depth of Poverty

36. Poverty Severity

  • Poverty-severity measures give greater weight to persons who are further below the poverty line.
📌 Must-Memorise

Headcount → Incidence

Gap → Depth

Severity → Deepest Poverty

37. Multidimensional Poverty — Meaning

  • Multidimensional poverty measures simultaneous deprivation across several aspects of life.
  • It captures deprivation that monetary measures may miss.

38. Why Multidimensional Measurement Is Important

Income improvement alone does not automatically guarantee access to:

  • Schools.
  • Hospitals.
  • Sanitation.
  • Water.
  • Electricity.
  • Housing.
  • Multidimensional measurement identifies both who is deprived and in which dimensions.

39. National Multidimensional Poverty Index — MPI

  • NITI Aayog is responsible for India's National Multidimensional Poverty Index framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

National MPI → NITI Aayog

40. National MPI — Three Dimensions

India's National MPI uses:

1. Health.

2. Education.

3. Standard of Living.

📌 Must-Memorise

MPI → Health + Education + Standard of Living

41. National MPI — 12 Indicators

Health:

  • Nutrition.
  • Child and adolescent mortality.
  • Maternal health.

Education:

  • Years of schooling.
  • School attendance.

Standard of Living:

  • Cooking fuel.
  • Sanitation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Electricity.
  • Housing.
  • Assets.
  • Bank account.
📌 Must-Memorise

National MPI → 3 Dimensions + 12 Indicators

42. MPI Formula — Basic Concept

  • MPI considers both the proportion of multidimensionally poor people and the intensity of their deprivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

MPI = Headcount Ratio × Intensity

43. India — MPI Decline

According to the supplied NITI Aayog figures:

  • 2015–16 → 24.85%.
  • 2019–21 → 14.96%.
📌 Must-Memorise

India MPI → 24.85% to 14.96%

44. India — Extrapolated MPI for 2022–23

According to the supplied source:

  • NITI Aayog estimated multidimensional poverty at 11.28% in 2022–23.
  • This was an extrapolated estimate rather than a direct headcount from a separate NFHS round.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

11.28% → Extrapolated Estimate

45. People Estimated to Have Exited Multidimensional Poverty

  • The supplied source states that approximately 24.82 crore people were estimated to have moved out of multidimensional poverty between 2013–14 and 2022–23.
📌 Must-Memorise

Estimated Exit from MPI → ≈24.82 Crore

46. Household Consumption Expenditure Survey — 2023–24

According to the supplied source, average nominal MPCE excluding imputed free welfare items was:

  • Rural India → ₹4,122.
  • Urban India → ₹6,996.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

HCES MPCE Figure ≠ Poverty Line

47. Major Economic Causes of Poverty

Important causes include:

  • Low productivity.
  • Unemployment.
  • Underemployment.
  • Low human capital.
  • Unequal access to assets.
  • Social exclusion.
  • Indebtedness.
  • Economic shocks.

48. Low Productivity and Poverty

  • People may remain poor despite working long hours when they are employed in low-productivity activities.
  • This is important in traditional agriculture and informal work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment Alone ≠ Escape from Poverty

49. Human Capital Poverty Trap

Poor Education and Health

→ Low Skills and Productivity

→ Low Income

→ Poor Education and Health

  • This can create a self-reinforcing poverty cycle.

50. Indebtedness and Health Shocks

  • High-interest debt can absorb a large share of household income.
  • Ill health can simultaneously reduce earning capacity and increase medical expenditure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Health Shock → Income ↓ + Expenditure ↑

51. Inflation and Poverty

  • Inflation can disproportionately affect poor households because essential goods, especially food, form a larger share of their expenditure.

52. Natural Disasters and Poverty

Floods, droughts and cyclones can destroy:

  • Crops.
  • Houses.
  • Livelihood assets.
  • Households without savings or insurance are especially vulnerable.

53. Rural Poverty

Rural poverty is associated with:

  • Landlessness.
  • Small holdings.
  • Low farm productivity.
  • Seasonal work.
  • Agricultural risk.
  • Lack of non-farm jobs.
  • Weak infrastructure.
  • Limited services.

54. Land Ownership and Poverty

  • Owning land does not automatically prevent poverty.
  • Very small holdings may generate insufficient income.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Land Ownership ≠ Absence of Poverty

55. Rural Poverty — Diversification

Rural poverty reduction increasingly requires non-farm opportunities in:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
  • Services.
  • Rural enterprises.
📌 Must-Memorise

Livelihood Diversification → Lower Dependence on Seasonal Agriculture

56. Urban Poverty

Urban poor households may face:

  • Informal employment.
  • High housing costs.
  • Transport costs.
  • Food costs.
  • Health expenditure.
  • Poor housing.
  • Weak social security.

57. Rural vs Urban Poverty

Rural poverty:

  • Landlessness.
  • Small holdings.
  • Seasonal work.
  • Agricultural vulnerability.

Urban poverty:

  • Informal jobs.
  • High housing and service costs.
  • Migrant vulnerability.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Same Nominal Income ≠ Same Living Standard Everywhere

58. Vulnerable Groups

Groups with greater poverty risk may include:

  • Landless labourers.
  • Casual workers.
  • Informal workers.
  • Single-parent households.
  • Persons with disabilities.
  • Elderly persons without income security.
  • Socially excluded communities.
  • Migrant workers.
  • Homeless persons.

59. Intergenerational Poverty

A typical cycle is:

Poor Household

→ Malnutrition

→ Weak Education

→ Low Skills

→ Low-Paid Work

→ Poor Household

Breaking it requires early intervention in:

  • Nutrition.
  • Health.
  • Schooling.
  • Skills.
  • Higher education.

60. Poverty vs Vulnerability

  • Poverty describes current deprivation.
  • Vulnerability describes the risk of falling into poverty after a shock.

A household can be above the poverty line but highly vulnerable to:

  • Illness.
  • Job loss.
  • Crop failure.
  • Disaster.

61. Poverty vs Unemployment vs Inequality

  • Poverty → Inadequate resources or living standards.
  • Unemployment → Inability to obtain work under labour-market definitions.
  • Inequality → Differences in income, wealth, consumption or opportunity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Poverty ≠ Unemployment ≠ Inequality

62. Working Poverty

  • A person may be employed and still remain poor because wages or productivity are too low.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employed Person Can Still Be Poor

63. Poverty Reduction vs Inequality Reduction

  • Poverty can fall while inequality rises.
  • Poor households may cross the poverty line even while richer households gain much faster.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Poverty Reduction ≠ Elimination of Inequality

64. Inclusive Growth and Anti-Poverty Strategy

India's broad anti-poverty strategy combines:

  • Economic growth.
  • Productive employment.
  • Human capital.
  • Food security.
  • Housing and basic services.
  • Financial inclusion.
  • Social protection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Growth + Jobs + Human Capital + Basic Services + Social Protection

65. Major Anti-Poverty Policy Links

Important strategic examples include:

  • MGNREGA → Employment and income.
  • DAY-NRLM → Sustainable rural livelihoods.
  • National Food Security Act, 2013 → Food security.
  • Education and health → Human-capital development.
  • Financial inclusion → Banking, credit, insurance and transfers.
  • Social assistance → Protection against old age, disability and income shocks.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Food Security Act → 2013

66. Dynamic Poverty

  • Poverty is not always permanent.
  • Households can move into and out of poverty.
  • Temporary illness, job loss or disaster can reverse earlier gains.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poverty → Dynamic, Not Always Permanent

67. Regional and Climate Vulnerability

National averages can hide differences across:

  • States.
  • Districts.
  • Rural and urban areas.
  • Social groups.

Climate change can increase poverty through:

  • Crop loss.
  • Heat stress.
  • Flooding.
  • Water scarcity.
  • Livelihood disruption.

68. Tamil Nadu — Multidimensional Poverty

According to NITI Aayog figures in the supplied source:

  • 2015–16 → 4.76%.
  • 2019–21 → 2.20%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu MPI → 4.76% to 2.20%

69. Tamil Nadu — Extrapolated MPI 2022–23

  • The supplied NITI Aayog discussion-paper estimate projected Tamil Nadu's multidimensional poverty headcount at approximately 1.43% in 2022–23.
  • It is an extrapolated estimate, not a separate direct NFHS headcount.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tamil Nadu 1.43% → Extrapolated Estimate

70. Tamil Nadu — Factors Associated with Lower MPI

The source associates Tamil Nadu's lower multidimensional poverty with a combination of:

  • Urbanisation.
  • Industrialisation.
  • Public health.
  • Education.
  • Nutrition programmes.
  • Social welfare.
  • Public distribution.
  • Women's development initiatives.
  • Poverty reduction should not be attributed to one single programme.

71. Tamil Nadu — Remaining Vulnerability

Even with relatively low overall MPI, deprivation can remain among:

  • Informal workers.
  • Migrant workers.
  • Urban poor.
  • Vulnerable elderly persons.
  • Remote rural communities.
  • Persons with disabilities.
  • Socially marginalised households.

72. Tamil Nadu — Future Poverty Challenge

The future challenge increasingly involves:

  • Preventing households from falling back into poverty.
  • Improving employment security.
  • Strengthening health protection.
  • Monitoring nutrition, housing, education and sanitation.
  • Protecting vulnerable groups from shocks.

  • Naoroji → Colonial poverty analysis.
  • Alagh → Calorie norms.
  • Lakdawala → State-specific calorie-linked lines.
  • Tendulkar → Broader consumption approach.
  • Rangarajan → Higher normative basket.
  • NITI Aayog → Multidimensional Poverty Index.

  • Tamil Nadu extrapolated 2022–23 → 1.43%.
